name: Electric toothbrush whitening heads
lead: Electric toothbrush whitening heads are replacement brush heads marketed for powered toothbrushes to remove surface stains and make teeth look whiter. They typically differ from standard heads in bristle layout or a polishing cup or pad. People use them to keep the visible shade of their teeth brighter day to day, since stained teeth are a common reason people feel their smile looks dull.

Wikipedia describes extrinsic stain as sitting on the tooth surface and coming largely from smoking, tannin-rich drinks such as coffee, tea and red wine, and certain foods, and says it can often be removed by cleaning, while intrinsic stain lies within the tooth and is the main target of bleaching [2]. Whitening heads address the first kind.

Electric toothbrushes in general are described as removing more plaque and reducing gum inflammation than manual brushes in a 2014 Cochrane review, though the review authors questioned the clinical importance of the difference [1]. No published trial has tested whitening heads against standard heads.

paras: Powered toothbrushes are oscillating-rotating, sonic (typically 200 to 400 Hz) or ultrasonic [1]. Manufacturers sell heads labelled for whitening, often with polishing elements, and many sonic brushes include a whitening mode alongside daily care, sensitive teeth and tongue cleaning modes [1].
Electric brushes date to Tomlinson Moseley's Motodent patent in 1937 and Philippe-Guy Woog's Broxodent in 1954, with the first ultrasonic brush patented in the US in 1992 [1].

sections.h: What brushing can and cannot change
paras: Surface stains from coffee, tea, red wine and tobacco can be reduced by cleaning, while intrinsic discolouration within the tooth is not removable by cleaning and is what bleaching targets [2]. Whitening toothpastes, which use higher amounts of abrasives and detergents, can lighten tooth colour by one or two shades with continued use, according to Wikipedia [2]. Wikipedia also notes that overly abrasive whitening toothpastes can harm dental tissue [2].
Brushing too hard can damage enamel and gums, and some brushes include pressure sensors [1]. Manufacturers advise replacing heads about every three months [1].

No studies found specific to whitening heads. Broader research on electric versus manual brushing is summarised in a 2014 Cochrane review, which reported plaque reductions of 11 percent after one to three months and 21 percent after three months, and gum-inflammation reductions of 6 and 11 percent; only oscillating-rotating brushes consistently showed a statistically significant benefit [1].

card.summary: Polishing-style replacement heads for powered brushes; they can address surface stain, with no head-specific trials found.
card.note: Does not change intrinsic tooth colour.

quick.overview:
Whitening heads are replacement heads for electric toothbrushes, sold to lift surface stains.

No studies of the heads themselves were found; electric brushes overall show modest plaque benefits.
quick.mechanism: Polishing bristles or pads mechanically remove surface stain. They do not bleach internal tooth colour.
quick.risks: Heavy brushing pressure can harm enamel and gums. Heads are advised to be replaced about every three months.

chain: Polishing bristles or pad scrub the tooth surface during daily brushing
Surface (extrinsic) stain from coffee, tea, wine or tobacco is reduced
angle.text: The heads are used in ordinary brushing to lift surface stain so teeth look whiter, without bleach. Inner tooth colour is unchanged.
